newsitem.title: UK: British newspapers praise Clarke's prudent budget.
newsitem.headline: British newspapers praise Clarke's prudent budget.

text.p: British newspapers praised finance minister Kenneth Clarke's pre-election budget with its one point cut in basic income tax, describing it as sensible, prudent and modest with "a little something for everyone".
Business leaders also gave it their cautious approval, but some feared its impact on inflation could result in a rise in interest rates before the election due by next May.
"The chancellor of the exchequer (finance minister) delivered a solid budget speech that had a little something for everyone without taking risks with the economy," The Times said in an editorial.
"Those at the top and bottom of the income scale will be disproportionately better off from tax cuts, thus pleasing rich Tory (Conserservative) voters while assuaging their social tax threshold."
The top-selling Sun tabloid referred to Clarke's "balancing act to cut taxes, trim borrowing and increase spending in crucial areas."

The slash in the basic rate of income tax to 23 percent from 24 percent was part of overall tax cuts of 2.2 billion pounds ($3.67 billion). Clarke also announced cuts in public spending amounting to 1.7 billion.
But the good news was offset by hikes in indirect taxes on tobacco products, air passenger duty, petrol and insurance premiums and by closing tax loopholes used by companies.
"Income tax is cut to lowest for 60 years...but smokers, motorists and travellers pay the price," was how The Daily Telegraph summed it up.
"It is a bits-and-pieces budget, more skillful in its construction than powerful in its impact," said the Financial Times.
British shares prices reacted mildly to the news ending 13.8 points up at 4,068.4, but still 20 points lower than the day's high before Clarke's announced his budget.

The Independent newspaper accused Clarke of blatant electioneering, saying he produced a budget designed to woo middle class voters and assure the Conservatives, who are trailing in opinion polls, a fifth consecutive term in power.

"The chancellor has targeted the income tax cuts straight at the great mass of middle-income earners, including the many disaffected voters the Tories need to win back in time for the election," it said.
The Daily Mail claimed Clarke had satisfied the most obvious electoral demands, with more spending on the police, prisons, education and the health service.
Overall the budget held few surprises and much of its impact was diluted by an embarrassing leak, the worst in half a century, of budget documents to the Daily Mirror newspaper on Monday night.

While economists calculated the impact of the budget on British taxpayers, Prime Minister John Major's office confirmed on Tuesday that the police had been called in to discover who leaked the documents, one of the nation's most closely guarded secrets, to the press.
